nameStory: This unusual plant gets its name 'apple-of-Peru' from its round, papery seed pods that somewhat resemble small apples, combined with its South American origins (Peru being part of its native range). The scientific name Nicandra honors the ancient Greek poet Nicander of Colophon, who wrote about plants and their medicinal properties in his poems over 2,000 years ago.
description: Apple-of-Peru is a tall, bushy annual plant that can reach 3-5 feet in height with a spreading, branching habit. It produces delicate bell-shaped flowers that are pale blue to white, followed by distinctive inflated, papery husks that enclose the fruits. This member of the nightshade family has escaped cultivation and occasionally pops up in gardens and disturbed areas, though it remains quite uncommon in New England.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - round fruits enclosed in large, inflated, papery husks that feel dry and crinkly when mature, resembling tiny Chinese lanterns

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bell-shaped flowers about 1 inch across, pale blue to white with five petals, blooming singly from leaf joints on short stalks

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, oval leaves with wavy or slightly toothed edges, arranged alternately on the stem, with a soft texture that bruises easily

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall annual plant growing 3-5 feet high with multiple branching stems that spread outward, creating a bushy appearance

habitat: Apple-of-Peru prefers rich, well-drained soils in sunny locations and is most often found in cultivated areas like gardens, farm edges, and disturbed ground. It occasionally escapes cultivation but rarely establishes large populations, appearing more as scattered individual plants in waste areas and along roadsides.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge with their characteristic soft, oval leaves developing on branching stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their pale blue to white bell-shaped flowers throughout the season, with early fruits beginning to develop.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive papery husks fully inflate and dry out, becoming the most noticeable feature as flowers fade and plants prepare to die back.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, but the dried papery husks may persist on dead stems, rattling in the wind if not cleared away.

funFact: Apple-of-Peru flowers open in the morning but close by mid-afternoon each day - they're literally early birds and early sleepers, making them easy to miss if you're not looking at the right time of day!
confusionNotes: The papery husks might be confused with ground cherries or Chinese lantern plant, but apple-of-Peru's husks are much larger and more inflated, and the plant itself grows much taller and bushier than ground cherries.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it comes from Peru, apple-of-Peru is actually native to western South America more broadly. It's sometimes called 'shoo-fly plant' because it was once believed to repel flies, though this property is questionable.
compareHints: Apple-of-Peru is the only Nicandra species you'll encounter in New England. Among nightshade family members, it's distinguished by its large, inflated papery husks - much bigger than those of ground cherries and without the orange color of Chinese lantern plant. The combination of pale blue flowers and large papery fruits makes it unique in the region.
